To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sodium–calcum exchanger undergoes a rapid conformational change in response to changes in intracellular calcium, and this change can be detected by the electrical currents it produces.
the Na– Ca exchanger undergoes two conformation changes that move charge across the cell membrane and that the exchanger is present in large numbers on the cell membrane and undergoes rapid turnover.
the sodium-calcium exchange protein is an electrogenic ion pump and that it is the principal mechanism for regulating intracellular calcium concentration in the cardiac myocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of the Na–Ca exchange.
the role of calcium in the control of cardiac muscle contraction, and the molecular mechanisms underlying this control.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the function of ion pumps, channels and transporters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Na– Ca exchanger is a molecular machine that moves charge and transports Na and Ca ions in a coordinated fashion, and is capable of operating at very high rates.
the Na– Ca exchanger is an electrogenic ion pump that is responsible for the rapid extrusion of Ca2+ from the cytoplasm of the cell and that it is capable of moving up to 2500 Ca2+ ions per second.
